whatIs: Hypothyroidism is a highly common endocrine disorder characterized by an underactive thyroid gland that fails to produce adequate amounts of essential thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). The thyroid gland, located at the front of the neck, is the body's metabolic engine, regulating how cells utilize energy. When thyroid hormone levels drop too low, the body's metabolic processes begin to significantly slow down. Because these hormones affect virtually every organ system, an underactive thyroid can lead to a wide and sometimes confusing array of physical and mental symptoms that develop gradually over months or even years.

The symptoms of hypothyroidism directly reflect the slowing of the body's metabolism. One of the most prominent signs is profound, persistent fatigue that does not improve with adequate sleep. Patients frequently experience unexplained weight gain or an inability to lose weight despite dietary efforts, increased sensitivity to cold, and persistent constipation. Physical changes often include dry and coarse skin, brittle nails, thinning hair, a puffy face, and hoarseness in the voice. Women with hypothyroidism may also notice heavier than normal or highly irregular menstrual periods.

Beyond the physical manifestations, hypothyroidism can take a substantial toll on a person's cognitive and emotional well-being. Individuals often describe feeling mentally sluggish, experiencing brain fog, memory difficulties, and a lack of concentration. Depression, persistent low mood, and a general loss of motivation are also strongly correlated with low thyroid hormone levels. Because these symptoms can mimic the natural aging process or clinical depression, proper medical evaluation and a simple blood test measuring TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) levels are essential for an accurate diagnosis.
causes: The leading cause of hypothyroidism worldwide, particularly in areas with adequate dietary iodine, is Hashimoto's thyroiditis. This is an autoimmune disorder in which the body's immune system erroneously produces antibodies that attack and progressively destroy the thyroid gland's tissue. This chronic inflammation slowly degrades the gland's ability to produce sufficient thyroid hormones. Hashimoto's tends to run in families, indicating a strong genetic predisposition, and it is significantly more prevalent in women than in men. The exact trigger that initiates this autoimmune cascade is still an area of active medical research.

Another frequent cause of hypothyroidism is the medical treatment required for hyperthyroidism. Individuals who have been treated with radioactive iodine or anti-thyroid medications to suppress an overactive thyroid, or those who have undergone surgical removal of a portion or all of the thyroid gland (thyroidectomy), will often naturally develop hypothyroidism as a result. In these instances, the underactive thyroid is an expected and permanent consequence of necessary medical intervention, requiring lifelong hormone replacement to maintain metabolic function.

Several other factors can contribute to an underactive thyroid. A severe deficiency of iodine in the diet is a primary cause globally, as iodine is an essential building block for thyroid hormones. Certain medications, including lithium (used for psychiatric disorders) and amiodarone (used for heart arrhythmias), can interfere with thyroid function and induce hypothyroidism. Less commonly, hypothyroidism can stem from a failure of the pituitary gland, a benign pituitary tumor, or a congenital defect where a baby is born with a defective or absent thyroid gland, making routine newborn screening vital.
